label: GPT-6 Astra
output:
Jess texted me last night: “It’s one assignment, don’t torch your job over it.”

I know, Jess. I really do.

We met student teaching in 2012. You have seen me try to look like I knew what I was doing in front of a room full of teenagers. There is no version of this where I get to convince you that I’m fearless, or particularly good at knowing when to shut up. And I know your text was not a statement about the importance of teaching history. It was a friend saying, Please don’t get hurt doing this.

Half the group chat agreed with you. Rather than send everyone fifteen increasingly long texts, I’m going to try to explain myself here.

The assignment is for my juniors in US History II, both sections. They interview someone in their family or neighborhood about Boston’s busing and desegregation years, 1974–76: a ten-minute recording and a two-page reflection. I’ve done it for four years. Until now, there hadn’t been a complaint.

That doesn’t automatically make it a good assignment. Four years without a complaint can mean things are working. It can also mean someone was uncomfortable and didn’t tell me.

This parent did tell someone. She emailed the principal and copied a school committee member. She said the project “reopens wounds” and “pressures kids to judge their grandparents.”

My first reaction was defensive. I’m attached to this project. I’ve seen what students do with it. But once I got past the part where I wanted to explain why she was wrong, I had to admit that her second point, especially, was fair.

An assignment can say “interview someone in your family or neighborhood” and still land as: Go ask your grandmother some difficult questions, record her answers, and bring them to school for a grade.

I’m the teacher. I know what I intend. That doesn’t mean a sixteen-year-old hears all the choices I think I’ve offered. It also doesn’t mean they feel free to say, This is going to cause trouble at home, and I don’t want to explain that trouble to you.

So yes, I need to change that part.

What I don’t think follows is that I need to drop the project.

The principal would like me to quietly let it go. We have a meeting with the parent on Thursday, November 19, at 3:15. My plan is to go in with an alternative built into the assignment: students can interview a librarian or archivist, or work with recordings from previous years where we have permission to use them. Nobody has to interview a family member. Nobody has to make their family’s private history available to me or to their classmates.

I want those options to be ordinary choices, not exceptions a kid has to earn by telling me something painful.

That seems like a real response to the complaint. I’m not going into the meeting to defeat this parent. She noticed a problem I should have thought through more carefully. I can take that seriously without agreeing that the whole thing needs to disappear.

Here’s why I want to keep it.

In 2023, a student interviewed his grandmother. She had driven a school bus in Southie in 1974. She’d never told anyone in the family.

He played about forty seconds of the interview for the class. Afterward, nobody said anything for what felt like a minute.

I’m not going to pretend I know what every student was thinking in that silence. Teachers can get carried away describing those moments. Sometimes a quiet classroom means something has landed; sometimes it means nobody wants to speak first.

But I remember it. We were listening to somebody’s grandmother talk about work she had actually done, in a place these kids knew, during something the textbook gives about a paragraph. And her grandson was hearing a part of her life he hadn’t known existed.

That’s worth making room for.

Last year, another student found out that her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus. She was upset. We talked after class twice. Her reflection was the best thing I read all year.

I hesitate even to put those two sentences next to each other, because her being upset wasn’t what made the paper good. I don’t get to count a kid’s distress as evidence that my teaching is working. She was the one who had to go home with that knowledge. I got to read the paper.

What mattered was the care she took with what she had learned. I don’t want to share her words here. They’re hers. But she was doing difficult historical thinking about a person she knew, and there wasn’t an easy answer she could give just to get it over with.

I need to leave room for a student to do that work. I also need to leave room for another student to say, I’m not doing it through my own family.

I’ve caught myself saying that the kids who are uncomfortable are the ones who need this most. There’s something in that instinct I still believe: discomfort isn’t always a sign that we should stop. Learning something you wish weren’t true can be part of learning history.

But as a rule for deciding what other people’s children ought to endure, it’s much too convenient for me.

I can require them to study desegregation. I can ask them to examine evidence, question an account, and support what they write. I can’t require a family reckoning. That’s the line I need to make clearer.

And this is the history of the city they live in. It happened on streets they know. People who lived through it are still here. Some want to talk; some don’t. Even that is something an oral history project can teach, provided we respect the answer.

A textbook paragraph can give them a few facts. It can’t do everything a voice can do. That doesn’t make a recorded memory the whole truth, either. Memories need questions and context. That’s part of the assignment, too.

Now, about the job.

You aren’t wrong. I’ve had tenure since 2021, but tenure doesn’t mean nothing can happen to me. The principal still controls my schedule and who gets AP. There are ways for work to become harder without anyone firing you.

I’m a little scared about Thursday. I would much rather have a normal afternoon than sit in a meeting knowing the easiest way to make everyone happy is to agree to stop doing something I think is valuable.

I also know that I’m asking you to understand a risk you can’t make smaller for me. You left teaching in 2019, but you haven’t forgotten what a school can ask of a person. I’m not going to treat your concern as if you’ve somehow stopped understanding because you work in HR now.

“It’s one assignment” is true. If I thought it couldn’t be done responsibly, I would need to let it go.

But I think it can. I think there’s a better version of it sitting right in front of us, one that takes the parent’s concern seriously and still lets students hear this history from people who lived it. I want to try that before I agree that the only sensible answer is to quit.

You don’t have to agree with me. I’d just like you to know I heard you, and that I’m not walking into Thursday looking for a fight.

I’ll text you after the meeting. You can tell me what you think. I’m still going to want to hear it.
